Therefore, clinical use of such predictive models requires careful validation to avoid unnecessary adaptation or insufficient correction.

Overall, AI has the potential to support adaptive proton therapy by accelerating multiple steps, including image reconstruction, segmentation, registration, dose verification, re-optimization, PSQA, and anatomical change prediction. However, the clinical value of AI in ART should ultimately be measured by whether it improves the speed, consistency, robustness, and safety of adaptive decisions. Future studies should move beyond isolated task performance and evaluate complete AI-assisted ART workflows using clinically meaningful endpoints, multi-institutional validation, and prospective testing where feasible. This is especially important in proton therapy because errors from image generation, registration, contouring, dose calculation, and optimization can propagate into range assessment and adaptive replanning decisions.

sections.title: Large language models and multimodal AI in proton therapy treatment planning

paragraphs.en: LLMs represent an emerging class of foundation models with strong capabilities in language understanding, summarization, information extraction, reasoning, and structured report generation.207, 208 Radiation oncology is well suited for LLM integration because many workflows rely on textual and structured information, including clinical notes, pathology and radiology reports, prescriptions, simulation orders, plan-evaluation narratives, and dose-volume constraints. Although LLMs do not directly solve the physical challenges of proton therapy, such as HU/RSP conversion, range uncertainty, MC dose calculation, or robust optimization, they may provide workflow-level support by integrating clinical context, standardizing documentation, assisting plan review, and improving communication among clinicians, physicists, dosimetrists, therapists, and patients.209, 210, 211, 212, 213, 214, 215, 216, 217, 218, 219, 220

A key technical strategy for clinical LLM deployment is grounding. General-purpose LLMs may generate plausible but incorrect responses when source-of-truth information is unavailable.207, 221 Therefore, modern clinical LLM systems increasingly use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG),222 tool-augmented agents,223, 224 supervised fine-tuning,214 and modular designs that separate deterministic calculations from natural-language generation.223 In radiation oncology, this is particularly relevant because many tasks can be anchored to structured information, such as dose-volume statistics, prescription data, structure nomenclature, protocol constraints, and electronic health record-derived clinical variables. For proton therapy, such grounding is essential because LLM-generated outputs should not independently determine dose calculation, plan approval, or adaptive replanning decisions; instead, they should support auditable decision-making by retrieving verified information, summarizing constraints, and communicating results in a clinically interpretable format.

Several LLM applications are directly relevant to proton therapy planning workflows (Figure 4). First, LLMs can support clinical data integration by extracting diagnosis, staging, prior treatment, modality, fractionation, and treatment-intent information from unstructured notes.225, 226 Fine-tuned open-source LLMs have been investigated for radiation oncology tasks such as treatment regimen generation, modality selection, and international classification of diseases 10th revision (ICD-10) prediction, demonstrating that domain-specific curation and supervised fine-tuning can improve performance compared with general models.214 In proton therapy, similar approaches may help identify planning-relevant clinical factors, such as re-irradiation history, prior dose, surgical status, implanted devices, or clinical indications for proton therapy.

Second, LLMs may improve standardization and plan evaluation. Structure nomenclature standardization is an important prerequisite for automated contouring, dose accumulation, multi-institutional research, and treatment-plan evaluation. LLM-based systems have been evaluated for relabeling radiotherapy structures according to AAPM TG-263,227 illustrating how guideline language can be translated into structured outputs. For proton therapy, standardized structure names and consistent clinical documentation are particularly valuable because downstream analyses may depend on accurate matching of targets, OARs, beam-path structures, and dose-volume endpoints. LLMs may also support protocol-aware plan evaluation by combining RAG, structured DVH data, and deterministic constraint-checking modules. In this setting, the LLM should summarize independently computed plan-quality metrics rather than generate dose values or autonomous clinical judgments.

Third, LLMs may assist routine workflow automation. Electronic health record-integrated systems have been used to draft patient-message responses, summarize CT simulation orders, generate daily readiness briefings, and support clinical trial matching.228, 229, 230 For proton therapy planning, the most relevant applications include summarizing simulation orders, standardizing setup and immobilization instructions, identifying prior radiation or pending imaging, and flagging patients who may require adaptive evaluation.208 These tools may reduce documentation burden and improve workflow consistency, particularly for complex patients requiring multidisciplinary coordination.

Fourth, emerging multimodal LLM systems may support contouring and treatment planning by integrating clinical text with imaging and dosimetric data.231, 232, 233, 234 Target delineation often depends on clinical context beyond image appearance alone, including tumor stage, laterality, surgical history, pathology, prior treatment, and physician intent. LLM-augmented multimodal segmentation frameworks may therefore improve target definition by incorporating patient-specific clinical information into image-based segmentation models.231, 232 Similarly, early studies have explored whether LLMs can assist treatment planning by interpreting DVH feedback and suggesting optimization parameter adjustments.233, 234 For proton therapy, such applications remain preliminary and require additional validation because any planning recommendation must remain compatible with proton beam geometry, spot delivery, range uncertainty, robustness requirements, and institutional planning practice.

Finally, safe clinical deployment of LLMs requires careful attention to failure modes, validation, privacy, and governance.221, 235, 236, 237 Common risks include hallucination, omission of key clinical details, inappropriate generalization, prompt sensitivity, overconfident wording, and vulnerability to untrusted inputs. These risks are especially important in proton therapy because incomplete or inaccurate clinical context could affect planning decisions, adaptive triage, or interpretation of prior dose and anatomical change. Therefore, LLM outputs should generally be treated as drafts, summaries, or decision-support information rather than autonomous clinical decisions. Practical safeguards include RAG-based grounding, source citation, deterministic constraint-checking, audit logs, secure deployment for protected health information, and human-in-the-loop review by clinicians and physicists.223

Overall, LLMs and multimodal foundation models should be viewed as workflow-support and clinical-intelligence tools that complement, rather than replace, physics-based AI models for proton therapy. Their near-term value lies in documentation, standardization, information retrieval, plan-review communication, adaptive workflow coordination, and patient engagement. Prospective validation, failure-mode analysis, privacy safeguards, and workflow-level evaluation will be necessary before routine clinical integration.

AI applications in proton therapy span multiple domains, including imaging, dose calculation, plan optimization, adaptive therapy, and treatment-planning QA. Each area shows encouraging progress, yet several overarching challenges remain. First, many DL models lack physical interpretability, which limits clinical trust and hinders safe deployment. Incorporating physics-informed constraints, such as dose kernels or MC approximations, can improve both robustness and transparency. This is particularly important for proton therapy, where visually plausible AI-generated images or dose distributions may still be clinically inadequate if they do not preserve RSP accuracy, proton range, or scenario-specific dose behavior. Therefore, future studies should report both conventional performance metrics and proton-specific dosimetric endpoints, including range error, DVH differences, gamma passing rates, and robustness metrics under setup and range uncertainty scenarios. Compared with photon therapy, these validation requirements are more stringent because proton dose distributions can be strongly affected by small errors in stopping power, anatomical heterogeneity, and beam-path anatomy.238

Second, uncertainty management remains particularly critical in proton therapy, where range uncertainty and anatomical change can substantially affect dose distributions. AI methods have been proposed for robustness evaluation,59, 171 scenario-specific dose prediction,60, 177 and robust dose mimicking,162, 177, 193 suggesting that AI may help identify plans vulnerable to uncertainty and accelerate robust plan adaptation. However, broader integration of AI-driven prediction with clinically validated robust optimization remains an active research area. Key unresolved questions include how to enforce physical consistency across uncertainty scenarios, propagate model uncertainty into robustness evaluation, and define acceptance criteria for AI-generated or AI-assisted robust plans. For adaptive proton therapy, these questions become even more important because image-generation errors, DIR uncertainty, contour uncertainty, and dose-calculation uncertainty may accumulate across the workflow and influence whether adaptation is triggered. Thus, AI-assisted proton therapy should be evaluated at the workflow level, not only at the level of isolated model outputs.

Third, the field suffers from limited availability of large, annotated datasets, restricting model generalizability across institutions and patient populations. This limitation is especially relevant for proton therapy because model performance can be affected by disease site, beam arrangement, delivery system, scanner type, reconstruction protocol, contouring practice, dose-calculation engine, and institutional planning philosophy. Many current studies remain retrospective, single-institutional, and disease-site specific.64 As a result, external validation, multi-institutional benchmarking, and transparent reporting of training data, validation cohorts, and clinical endpoints are essential before these tools can be adopted routinely. Studies should also clearly distinguish whether a model was developed specifically for proton therapy or adapted from photon/general radiotherapy applications, because adapted methods may require additional validation for RSP accuracy, range uncertainty, spot delivery, and robust optimization.

A recurring theme across this review is that many AI methods are shared between photon and proton therapy, but their clinical validation requirements differ. Image segmentation, DIR, dose prediction, sCT/reCT generation, and automated planning are important in both modalities. However, in photon therapy, errors often primarily affect local dose estimation, contour-based evaluation, or OAR/target dose metrics. In proton therapy, the same errors can also propagate into water-equivalent path length, beam range, distal-edge placement, scenario-specific dose, and robust optimization. Therefore, photon-derived AI tools provide valuable methodological foundations, but direct transfer to proton therapy usually requires additional inputs, such as HU/RSP maps, beam geometry, spot or energy-layer information, uncertainty scenarios, and proton-specific endpoints. This distinction should be considered when interpreting studies that are not proton-therapy-specific but are cited for methodological relevance.

Beyond conventional IMPT planning, AI may also contribute to emerging proton-specific applications, including proton arc therapy,239, 240 FLASH proton therapy,241, 242 LET-guided planning,243 range verification,244, 245, 246 and motion-adaptive delivery.247, 248 In proton arc therapy, AI may help navigate the enlarged optimization space created by many beam angles, energy layers, and spot trajectories. In FLASH proton therapy, AI may support rapid plan generation and evaluation under additional constraints related to dose rate, delivery time, normal-tissue sparing, and machine capability. AI may also support LET prediction, LET-guided optimization, motion-adaptive delivery, and range-verification methods such as proton-acoustic imaging.246 These applications remain early-stage but represent important proton-specific research directions in which AI may provide value beyond general radiotherapy automation.

As discussed in Section G, LLMs and multimodal AI may support workflow-level tasks, such as clinical-context extraction, protocol retrieval, planning documentation, plan-review assistance, adaptive workflow triage, and integration of textual clinical records with imaging and dosimetric information. However, these models must be distinguished from safety-critical models that directly affect dose calculation, optimization, or plan approval. Before clinical use in proton therapy decision support, LLMs and multimodal AI require rigorous validation, privacy protection, hallucination control, uncertainty quantification, failure-mode analysis, and integration into physician and physicist review workflows.

Another important consideration is the relationship between AI-based workflow acceleration and clinical responsibility. AI tools may reduce the time required for image reconstruction, DIR, auto-segmentation, dose calculation, plan optimization, and adaptive replanning, but faster workflows do not remove the need for independent verification.249 AI-generated sCT/reCT images, DIR results, contours, predicted doses, and spot weights should be reviewed against anatomical fidelity, dose-calculation usability, clinical objectives, robustness requirements, and deliverability. Thus, AI should currently be viewed as a decision-support and workflow-acceleration tool rather than a replacement for expert clinical judgment. This human-in-the-loop model is especially important in proton therapy because small model errors may have amplified downstream effects on range, robustness, and adaptive decisions.

Finally, while early studies demonstrate technical feasibility, few have undergone prospective validation, and regulatory pathways for AI adoption in radiation oncology are still evolving. Future directions should prioritize hybrid physics-AI frameworks, multimodal data integration, standardized evaluation benchmarks, and multi-institutional collaborations to ensure reproducibility, clinical reliability, and safe deployment. For proton therapy specifically, future research should emphasize proton-relevant endpoints, including RSP accuracy, range uncertainty, scenario-wise robustness, LET-related considerations where applicable, and the dosimetric impact of AI-generated inputs. Establishing such evaluation standards will be essential for moving AI-assisted proton therapy treatment planning from technical feasibility toward clinically reliable implementation. Ultimately, successful clinical translation will require not only accurate AI models but also workflow-level validation showing that AI improves planning efficiency, adaptive decision consistency, robustness, and patient safety.

AI holds strong potential to transform proton therapy by enabling faster, more consistent, and more adaptive treatment planning and delivery. Across the proton therapy planning chain, AI methods may support imaging, registration, segmentation, contour assessment, dose prediction and denoising, optimization, robustness evaluation, and adaptive replanning. LLMs and multimodal foundation models may further support documentation, clinical-context integration, and workflow coordination, but they should remain distinct from safety-critical dose calculation or plan-approval tasks. Widespread clinical adoption will require interpretable, physics-aware models; validation in large and diverse patient cohorts; and evaluation using proton-specific endpoints such as HU/RSP accuracy, range uncertainty, dose-calculation accuracy, robustness, deliverability, and adaptive decision consistency. With continued interdisciplinary collaboration and workflow-level validation, AI-assisted proton therapy can advance toward safer, more efficient, and more personalized cancer care.
